title: The Army Brought Machine Guns. The Emus Won. #shorts
description:
Case 040. In November 1932 about 20,000 emus moved into the wheatbelt of Western Australia after their breeding season and raided the farmers' crops. The farmers, many of them First World War veterans, asked the Minister of Defence, Sir George Pearce, for machine guns. Major G. P. W. Meredith of the Royal Australian Artillery went out with two soldiers, two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition. On 4 November an ambush on about a thousand emus at a farm dam ended when the gun jammed. A gun mounted on a truck could not keep up with the birds, and the ride was too rough to shoot. After six days and bad press the troops were withdrawn on 8 November; at the farmers' request they went back on 13 November, and the major was recalled for good in December. His report claimed 986 birds for 9,860 rounds: exactly ten rounds a bird. Those are his own figures. Later requests for military help were refused, and the farmers were left with bounties and fences. Rook didn't buy the arithmetic either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. No bird is shown hit or killed. The uniforms carry no badges or insignia, the truck no markings, the newspaper no headline, and nobody's likeness is attempted. Staging details such as the dam, the truck, the tent, the farm, the fence, the newspaper bundle and everything Rook does are reconstruction, not record. The major's words about tanks are quoted as the sources report them. Narration is a synthetic voice (Kokoro).

authoring.run: scheduled short run, 19 Nov 2026 (retry of an earlier attempt); the batch brief's ten Shorts are all authored, so this run took the first slate idea, case 040

story_score_note: Re-scored at authoring (slate estimate 95). Stakes are crops and an army's pride, not lives, so 6; the Emu War is a well-known internet story, so freshness 6, lifted by Rook's angle of auditing the major's suspiciously tidy figures; research 8 because the totals are the major's own claim. Curiosity 10, story 8 and payoff 8 clear the gate's 6.

source_notes: Read for this run on 19 Nov 2026 through a fetch tool: Wikipedia ('Emu War'), History Hit ('The Great Emu War', Kyle Hoekstra, 29 Mar 2023), Mental Floss ('When Australia Went to War With Its Emus', Paul Anthony Jones, 25 Aug 2016) and BBC Wildlife / Discover Wildlife ('The Emu War of 1932', Debbie Graham, 2 Feb 2026). Every narrated fact is on at least two of them. About 20,000 emus: all four. They came onto the farmland after the breeding season (Wikipedia; Discover Wildlife: after raising broods inland, migrating west for food and water). Farmers were ex-soldiers / First World War veterans: all four. They asked the Minister of Defence, Sir George Pearce, for machine guns: Wikipedia, History Hit, Mental Floss. Major G. P. W. Meredith, Royal Australian Artillery, two soldiers (Sgt S. McMurray, Gunner J. O'Halloran), two Lewis guns, 10,000 rounds: Wikipedia, History Hit, Mental Floss (Discover Wildlife: two Lewis guns, the major unnamed). Ambush on about a thousand emus at a dam or watering hole, the gunners waited until they were close, the gun jammed (after about a dozen birds): Wikipedia (4 November, 'more than 1,000', local dam), Mental Floss (watering hole, 1,000, within 100 yards, jammed after 12), History Hit (4 November, some 1,000, jam), Discover Wildlife (thousand-strong flock, jam); the narration does not mention any bird killed there and none is shown. Gun on a truck: the truck could not gain on the birds and the ride was too rough to fire: Wikipedia, History Hit, Mental Floss, Discover Wildlife. Withdrawn after six days and bad press: Wikipedia (2 to 8 November, after negative press coverage), Discover Wildlife ('after six days'), Mental Floss (barely a week, press reports), History Hit (8 November). The quote 'they can face machine guns with the invulnerability of tanks': Wikipedia (attributed to Meredith via the Sunday Herald, 1953), History Hit, Mental Floss, Discover Wildlife (unnamed major); the narration says 'the major says', not that it was in his report. Returned at the farmers' request on 13 November: Wikipedia, History Hit; Mental Floss 'later the same month'. Recalled about four weeks later: Wikipedia (10 December), Mental Floss (early December, 'a month later'). His totals, 986 birds and 9,860 rounds: Wikipedia, Mental Floss (both as Meredith's claim); 'exactly 10 rounds per confirmed kill': Wikipedia, History Hit. Later requests for the army refused: Wikipedia (1934, 1943, 1948), Mental Floss (1934), Discover Wildlife. Bounties: all four (Wikipedia: 57,034 claimed in six months of 1934). Fences: Wikipedia (exclusion fencing), Mental Floss (a five-foot emu-proof fence), Discover Wildlife (the barrier fence). Kept out because single-sourced, disputed or about suffering: the 2,500 'wounded' claim (Wikipedia calls it highly disputed; Mental Floss says 'more than 2000'), the dozen birds killed at the dam, the 100 emu skins for hats, the Zulu comparison, the cinematographer, the secession theory, the 1950 ammunition release, the bounty count. The labels 4 NOVEMBER 1932 and 13 NOVEMBER are on Wikipedia and History Hit; DECEMBER 1932 is used instead of 10 December because only Wikipedia gives the day. Staging that is not fact: the look of the dam, the spoil bank, the truck, the gun mount, the tent and its contents, the newspaper bundle (no headline), the telegram and the letter, the farm, the windmills, the fence-building, the number and placement of emus in every shot, and everything Rook does.

experiments.E1_E2: spine v2: Rook is already beside the jammed gun in shot 5 and doubts it in one line of 1.4 s ('Beaten by birds? No chance.') with the emus scattering behind him; no office. The story runs forward from the ambush; date, place and name are on-screen labels (4 NOVEMBER 1932, W. AUSTRALIA, 1932, MAJOR MEREDITH).
experiments.E3: The batch brief's ten Shorts are all authored, so this Short is outside the batch. It opens on the wide spectacle (the mob running at the lens), the opposite of the previous Short (r025, close-up).
experiments.E4: Question ending tied to a real open point (the major's own figures): 'Ten a bird, exactly. Do you buy it?'
experiments.E8: tail 0.4 s; the last line ('I keep picturing') runs into the first ('a thousand emus, heading for a hidden machine gun'), and the last shot is the opening played back to its first frame.
experiments.rook_action: Detective actions in the story world: he raps the jammed gun (5), knocks on an emu's chest to test the 'tanks' line (16), and lays brass cases out in rows of ten to check the major's arithmetic (23). Mannerisms: hat brim low (5, 14), hat bouncing off his head on the truck (11), eyes over the newspaper with one brow up (13), brim dropping over his eyes (16), beak tap (23), lifting the brim with one finger (24), flinching at the hammer (26), flipping the brass case like a coin and pocketing it as the case's shiny object (29).

sound_plan.first_frame: A low 'boom' at 0.05 of the first shot for the drumming feet of the mob (the gate needs an impact in the first second; here it is a story sound), then a scratch; the music under the hook is the near-silent 'hook' mood.
sound_plan.music: The engine's score follows the segment moods: hook, tense for Rook's line, action for the chase, calm for the retreat, tense for the re-hook, action for the count, wonder for 'suspiciously tidy', end for the question. No tragic beats in this story.
sound_plan.effects: One to four cues a shot, each tied to something visible: pops for the two bursts (no realistic gunfire), clunks and a sputter for the jam, engine starts and a horn for the truck, flips for the newspapers, the telegram and the letter, scratches for the pen, ticks for the counting, clunks for the hammer.
sound_plan.hush: Shot 22 (the brass pouring out of the box): the music drops out for the breath before 'Exactly ten rounds a bird.'
sound_plan.voice: Narration is ducked over the bed by the engine; measured in the local rehearsal, not listened to.
